The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical methods (DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, BiScope \cite{guo2024_biscope}, GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr}, Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster}, DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt}), geometric approaches based on intrinsic dimensionality \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark}, with known limits from paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and generator barriers \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval}, RAID \cite{dugan2024_raid}, and MAGE \cite{li2024_mage} benchmark detection across domains, models, and adversarial conditions.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects whether text appeared in pretraining data by selecting tokens with the lowest model probabilities, a token-level statistical approach related to our passage-level perplexity features.

\citet{christ2024_undetectable} show that watermarks can be made cryptographically undetectable, but all watermarking approaches require proactive cooperation from the generator; our method operates retroactively on unmodified text.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails; \citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this via scaling laws \cite{seddik2024synthetic}, \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends the analysis to self-consuming models.
Subsequent work addresses mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated,wenzek2020_ccnet}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, convergence and stability \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,knowledge_collapse2025,dohmatob2024_demystified,bertrand2024_stability}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,briesch2024selfconsuming,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral,synthetic_eggs2026}.
\citet{bertrand2024_stability} prove that iterative retraining on mixed real-synthetic data converges to a fixed point, providing theoretical grounding for the distributional saturation underlying our EDD ceiling (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}).
\citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, complementing the tail-erosion view we operationalize.
\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple distinct phenomena, and call for operationally precise metrics.
Dohmatob et al.\ predict that recursive training erodes distributional tails as a theoretical scaling law \citep{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}; we operationalize this prediction into a deployable ordinal classifier, revealing strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical methods (DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, BiScope \cite{guo2024_biscope}, GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr}, Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster}, DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt}), geometric approaches based on intrinsic dimensionality \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark}, with known limits from paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and generator barriers \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval}, RAID \cite{dugan2024_raid}, and MAGE \cite{li2024_mage} benchmark detection across domains, models, and adversarial conditions.
\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish authorship attribution (which model?) from verification (human or AI?); depth estimation introduces a third axis: which recursive iteration.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects whether text appeared in pretraining data by selecting tokens with the lowest model probabilities, a token-level statistical approach related to our passage-level perplexity features.
However, membership inference answers a binary question (in training data or not) without addressing recursive depth.
\citet{christ2024_undetectable} show that watermarks can be made cryptographically undetectable, but all watermarking approaches require proactive cooperation from the generator; our method operates retroactively on unmodified text.
Depth estimation thus occupies a distinct niche: ordinal, retroactive, and cooperation-free.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains; \citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text; LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, characterizing \emph{how} text degrades without classifying which iteration a passage comes from.
Our task performs the inverse, ordinal depth estimation from text alone, discriminating between adjacent depths rather than merely detecting aggregate degradation.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal classification has a long history \cite{mccullagh1980_ordinal}: \citet{frank2001} reduce ordinal problems to nested binary tasks, and \citet{rennie2005} introduce loss functions tailored to discrete ordered labels.
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses; \citet{kasa2024_ordinality} benchmark explicit and implicit ordinal techniques for NLP tasks; \citet{janitza2016_ordinal_rf} analyze Random Forest behavior on ordinal targets, showing that standard RF implicitly respects ordinal structure when inter-class distances are monotonic.
We adopt CORAL and CLOC as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus,finlayson2024_closing,garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded,wiher2022_decoding,basu2021_mirostat}.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation: temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal, effects beyond single-pass text quality.

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation can be modeled as iterative density estimation: each depth-$k$ model approximates the distribution of $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, which was itself sampled from the depth-$(k{-}1)$ model.
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} show that this process contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first.
If $p_k$ denotes the token distribution at depth $k$, the tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in $k$ for large $t$.
This tail erosion predicts \texttt{p90\_ppl} as a depth marker: the 90th-percentile perplexity captures exactly the region where successive generations remove probability mass.
Our data confirm this prediction: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks top-2 in all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}), and fine-tuning loss decreases monotonically with depth for all three families.
Surprisal variance captures the complementary signal of distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterize model collapse via exponential tail decay: tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ that depends on model capacity and data size.
Since the dominant features track tail mass and tail mass contracts geometrically, the pairwise AUC-excess should contract at a comparable rate; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below the classifier's resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay but with a decreasing ratio, as the distribution approaches a fixed point where residual variation falls below the feature resolution \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
5-class extensions to d4 for all three families (71--80\% accuracy, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm that depth~4 remains discriminable in the multi-class setting; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics at this depth, and the saturation of aggregate statistics places a physical ceiling on discriminability.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
The contraction factor $\alpha$ depends on model capacity: larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step, so the per-step distributional shift is smaller ($\alpha$ closer to 1).
EDD should therefore decrease with generator scale, since the feature distance between adjacent depths shrinks below classifier resolution at shallower depths.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 pairwise AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}), consistent with the first recursive step at higher capacity: the 14B model produces a near-faithful copy of its training distribution, and the residual distributional shift is detectable only through higher-order feature statistics.

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

This paper formalizes recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and provides both theoretical grounding (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}) and empirical characterization across three 1--1.5B base model families and three decoding strategies in controlled settings.
The tail erosion mechanism and strategy-dependent convergence rates predicted in \S\ref{sec:method:theory} are confirmed across the atlas; five features suffice for 97.6\% of full performance, consistent with the low effective dimensionality of the degradation process.
Extending all three families to d4 yields 71--80\% five-class accuracy (chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}); aggregate statistics (mean perplexity) saturate before tail statistics at this depth, and this saturation provides a physical explanation for the EDD ceiling.

Cross-strategy transfer is the primary bottleneck (d1--d3: 45.9\%, chance = 33\%), with d1/d2 boundary inversion under strategy mismatch revealing that different decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories; a proof-of-concept two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp.
For data curation, RF filtering (F1\,=\,0.997) outperforms perplexity thresholds (F1\,=\,0.845) for depth identification, but downstream training improvement is non-significant ($p > 0.4$; Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}, \ref{app:downstream}).
In principle, depth estimation could complement C2PA \cite{c2pa2024} and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} by providing a retroactive, cooperation-free signal; cross-model chains (84.75\%) confirm the signal is process-level, though deployment beyond controlled settings requires addressing cross-strategy transfer.
The weakest link is d2 recall (26.8\% under cross-model transfer); BOS-seeded generation was validated under prompted conditions for only 1/9 cells ($-$13.8\,pp; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).
Cross-strategy transfer and depth-quality entanglement remain open challenges (Limitations; Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}).

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
5	Recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails \cite{shumailov2024_nature}, an effect formalized as exponential tail decay via scaling laws \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,seddik2024synthetic} and extended to autophagous loops in the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad}.
6	Subsequent work refines the conditions under which collapse occurs: \citet{bertrand2024_stability} identify convergence to a fixed point under mixed real-synthetic retraining (providing theoretical grounding for our EDD ceiling, \S\ref{sec:method:theory}), \citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, and \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} extend guarantees to broader model classes.
7	Mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated,wenzek2020_ccnet}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, convergence analysis \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,knowledge_collapse2025,dohmatob2024_demystified}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,briesch2024selfconsuming,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral,synthetic_eggs2026} are active areas.
8	\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple phenomena and call for operationally precise metrics; we respond by operationalizing tail-erosion predictions into a deployable ordinal classifier, revealing strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
9	All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.
10	
11	\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
12	The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical methods (DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, BiScope \cite{guo2024_biscope}, GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr}, Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster}, DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt}), geometric approaches based on intrinsic dimensionality \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark}, with known limits from paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and generator barriers \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
13	M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval}, RAID \cite{dugan2024_raid}, and MAGE \cite{li2024_mage} benchmark detection across domains, models, and adversarial conditions.
14	\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish authorship attribution (which model?) from verification (human or AI?); depth estimation introduces a third axis: which recursive iteration.
15	All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.
16	
17	\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
18	Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects whether text appeared in pretraining data by selecting tokens with the lowest model probabilities, a token-level statistical approach related to our passage-level perplexity features.
19	However, membership inference answers a binary question (in training data or not) without addressing recursive depth.
20	\citet{christ2024_undetectable} show that watermarks can be made cryptographically undetectable, but all watermarking approaches require proactive cooperation from the generator; our method operates retroactively on unmodified text.
21	Depth estimation thus occupies a distinct niche: ordinal, retroactive, and cooperation-free.
22	
23	\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
24	EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains; \citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text; LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities.
25	\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, characterizing \emph{how} text degrades without classifying which iteration a passage comes from.
26	Our task performs the inverse, ordinal depth estimation from text alone, discriminating between adjacent depths rather than merely detecting aggregate degradation.
27	
28	\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
29	Ordinal classification has a long history \cite{mccullagh1980_ordinal}: \citet{frank2001} reduce ordinal problems to nested binary tasks, and \citet{rennie2005} introduce loss functions tailored to discrete ordered labels.
30	CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses; \citet{kasa2024_ordinality} benchmark explicit and implicit ordinal techniques for NLP tasks; \citet{janitza2016_ordinal_rf} analyze Random Forest behavior on ordinal targets, showing that standard RF implicitly respects ordinal structure when inter-class distances are monotonic.
31	We adopt CORAL and CLOC as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.
32	
33	\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
34	Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus,finlayson2024_closing,garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded,wiher2022_decoding,basu2021_mirostat}.
35	Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation: temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal, effects beyond single-pass text quality.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$); a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is therefore needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}
In strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.
A two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\,pp vs.\ Pythia $+$8.0\,pp).
Practical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$97\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), a design that isolates the depth variable but diverges from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.
Domain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Cross-scale experiments (7--14B, \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show signal that attenuates with scale; at 14B, d0/d1 separability nearly vanishes ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}0$) while d1--d3 discrimination persists; this constitutes a boundary condition for the current feature set (confounded by self-reference model; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_confounds}).
A base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.
Segment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open (Appendix~\ref{app:mixed_depth}); in particular, partial mixing (accumulation), where a single document contains fragments from different recursive depths, is a key open question, as our framework assumes uniform depth per passage.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), per-model FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
A pooled RF classifier evaluated on larger corpora (10{,}000 passages each) yields 34\% FPR on C4 and 17\% on FineWeb \cite{penedo2024_fineweb}; the gap reflects quality filtering in FineWeb removing feature-anomalous text that triggers false positives.
Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0).
Confidence thresholding ($P(\mathrm{d0}) \geq 0.15$) reduces pooled FPR from 34\%/17\% to 2.8\%/0.7\% on C4/FineWeb at minimal accuracy cost ($-$0.3\,pp); high FPR is therefore a decision-threshold problem, not a fundamental calibration defect, though the optimal threshold remains domain-dependent (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Reference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\times$ chance.
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\%); the overlap therefore does not confer a systematic advantage.
An ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\Delta{\leq}$11\,pp).
The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.
Reference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\% (partial signal in lexical statistics) but trail the full pipeline by 25pp; surprisal-based features are therefore essential.
Simple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\% vs.\ 78.6\%).

\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}
Cross-seed replication covers 3 of 9 cells (Pythia, OLMo, GPT-2~XL nucleus); seed=43 yields $+$0.1 to $+$3.2\,pp higher accuracy, with 2/3 deltas statistically significant (non-overlapping CIs).
Feature rankings and depth ordering are consistent across seeds, but single-seed absolute accuracy carries ${\sim}$1--3\,pp uncertainty; cross-cell comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Depth signal scales with passage length (68.4\% at 128 tokens, 77.8\% at 512; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}), saturating near 500 tokens.
Prompted generation was validated on only 1 of 9 cells (GPT-2~XL nucleus); generalization to other model--strategy configurations under prompted conditions is not established.
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and curated synthetic data may not trigger collapse \cite{falahati2026_curated}, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.

\label{sec:discussion}

This paper formalizes recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and provides both theoretical grounding (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}) and empirical characterization across three 1--1.5B base model families and three decoding strategies in controlled settings.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
Recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails \cite{shumailov2024_nature}, an effect formalized as exponential tail decay via scaling laws \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,seddik2024synthetic} and extended to autophagous loops in the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad}.
Subsequent work refines the conditions under which collapse occurs: \citet{bertrand2024_stability} identify convergence to a fixed point under mixed real-synthetic retraining (providing theoretical grounding for our EDD ceiling, \S\ref{sec:method:theory}), \citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, and \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} extend guarantees to broader model classes.
Mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated,wenzek2020_ccnet}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, convergence analysis \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,knowledge_collapse2025,dohmatob2024_demystified}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,briesch2024selfconsuming,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral,synthetic_eggs2026} are active areas.
\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple phenomena and call for operationally precise metrics; we respond by operationalizing tail-erosion predictions into a deployable ordinal classifier, revealing strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}

M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval}, RAID \cite{dugan2024_raid}, and MAGE \cite{li2024_mage} benchmark detection across domains, models, and adversarial conditions.
\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish authorship attribution (which model?) from verification (human or AI?); depth estimation introduces a third axis: which recursive iteration.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\citet{christ2024_undetectable} show that watermarks can be made cryptographically undetectable, but all watermarking approaches require proactive cooperation from the generator; our method operates retroactively on unmodified text.

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation can be modeled as iterative density estimation: each depth-$k$ model approximates the distribution of $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, which was itself sampled from the depth-$(k{-}1)$ model.
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} show that this process contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first.
If $p_k$ denotes the token distribution at depth $k$, the tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in $k$ for large $t$.
This tail erosion predicts \texttt{p90\_ppl} as a depth marker: the 90th-percentile perplexity captures exactly the region where successive generations remove probability mass.
Our data confirm this prediction: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks top-2 in all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}), and fine-tuning loss decreases monotonically with depth for all three families.
Surprisal variance captures the complementary signal of distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterize model collapse via exponential tail decay: tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ that depends on model capacity and data size.
Since the dominant features track tail mass and tail mass contracts geometrically, the pairwise AUC-excess should contract at a comparable rate; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below the classifier's resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay but with a decreasing ratio, as the distribution approaches a fixed point where residual variation falls below the feature resolution \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
5-class extensions to d4 for all three families (71--80\% accuracy, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm that depth~4 remains discriminable in the multi-class setting; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics at this depth, and the saturation of aggregate statistics places a physical ceiling on discriminability.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
The contraction factor $\alpha$ depends on model capacity: larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step, so the per-step distributional shift is smaller ($\alpha$ closer to 1).
EDD should therefore decrease with generator scale, since the feature distance between adjacent depths shrinks below classifier resolution at shallower depths.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 pairwise AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}), consistent with the first recursive step at higher capacity: the 14B model produces a near-faithful copy of its training distribution, and the residual distributional shift is detectable only through higher-order feature statistics.

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first \cite{shumailov2024_nature}: tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in depth $k$.
This tail erosion predicts \texttt{p90\_ppl} as a depth marker, confirmed by its top-2 ranking in all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}).
Surprisal variance captures complementary distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
Tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below classifier resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay approaching a fixed point \cite{bertrand2024_stability}.
5-class extensions to d4 (71--80\%, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm depth~4 discriminability; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics, placing a physical ceiling on EDD.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
Larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step ($\alpha$ closer to 1), so EDD should decrease with scale.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}).

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
Recursive training on model outputs erodes distributional tails \cite{shumailov2024_nature}, an effect formalized as exponential tail decay via scaling laws \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails,seddik2024synthetic} and extended to autophagous loops in the MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad}.
Subsequent work refines the conditions under which collapse occurs: \citet{bertrand2024_stability} identify convergence to a fixed point under mixed real-synthetic retraining (providing theoretical grounding for our EDD ceiling, \S\ref{sec:method:theory}), \citet{shi2025_closer_look} reframe collapse as a generalization-to-memorization transition, and \citet{dohmatob2025_strong_collapse} extend guarantees to broader model classes.
Mitigation \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate,drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse,yi2026_escaping_collapse,falahati2026_curated,wenzek2020_ccnet}, non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, convergence analysis \cite{marchi2024_heat_death,wang2026_contamination,knowledge_collapse2025,dohmatob2024_demystified}, and diversity decline \cite{guo2024curious,briesch2024selfconsuming,padmakumar2024diversity,sigma2026_spectral,synthetic_eggs2026} are active areas.
\citet{schaeffer2025} argue that ``model collapse'' conflates multiple phenomena and call for operationally precise metrics; we respond by operationalizing tail-erosion predictions into a deployable ordinal classifier, revealing strategy-dependent trajectories and non-monotonic 7B behavior that the theory does not predict.
All assume depth is known a priori; we address the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
The detection literature \cite{wu2025_detection_survey} spans statistical methods (DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, DivEye \cite{diveye2026}, BiScope \cite{guo2024_biscope}, GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr}, Ghostbuster \cite{verma2024_ghostbuster}, DNA-GPT \cite{yang2024_dnagpt}), geometric approaches based on intrinsic dimensionality \cite{tulchinskii2023_intrinsic_dim}, and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark}, with known limits from paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase}, distribution shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and generator barriers \cite{pu2026_generator_barrier}.
M4-SemEval \cite{wang2024_m4_semeval}, RAID \cite{dugan2024_raid}, and MAGE \cite{li2024_mage} benchmark detection across domains, models, and adversarial conditions.
\citet{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms} distinguish authorship attribution (which model?) from verification (human or AI?); depth estimation introduces a third axis: which recursive iteration.
All these methods perform binary classification, discarding ordinal depth information; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Membership Inference and Data Provenance.}
Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} detects pretraining membership via low-probability token statistics, related to our perplexity features but limited to binary classification; cryptographically undetectable watermarks \cite{christ2024_undetectable} require generator cooperation.
Depth estimation occupies a distinct niche: ordinal, retroactive, and cooperation-free.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates editing extent but does not model recursive chains; \citet{uchendu2020_attribution} classify \emph{which} model generated text; LOKI \cite{loki2025} benchmarks synthetic data detection across modalities.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, characterizing \emph{how} text degrades without classifying which iteration a passage comes from.
Our task performs the inverse, ordinal depth estimation from text alone, discriminating between adjacent depths rather than merely detecting aggregate degradation.

\paragraph{Ordinal Classification.}
Ordinal classification has a long history \cite{mccullagh1980_ordinal}: \citet{frank2001} reduce ordinal problems to nested binary tasks, and \citet{rennie2005} introduce loss functions tailored to discrete ordered labels.
CORAL \cite{coral2020} enforces rank consistency via ordered binary tasks; CLOC \cite{cloc2025} extends contrastive learning with multi-margin ordinal losses; \citet{kasa2024_ordinality} benchmark explicit and implicit ordinal techniques for NLP tasks; \citet{janitza2016_ordinal_rf} analyze Random Forest behavior on ordinal targets, showing that standard RF implicitly respects ordinal structure when inter-class distances are monotonic.
We adopt CORAL and CLOC as baselines (\S\ref{sec:generalization}) to confirm the signal is accessible to principled ordinal methods.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways that interact with depth signals \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus,finlayson2024_closing,garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded,wiher2022_decoding,basu2021_mirostat}.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation: temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal, effects beyond single-pass text quality.

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Problem Definition}
5	\label{sec:method:problem}
6	
7	Let $f_\theta$ denote a language model and $\mathcal{D}_0$ a corpus of human-written seed text.
8	We define a \emph{recursive generation chain} of depth $K$ as the sequence $\mathcal{D}_0, \mathcal{D}_1, \dots, \mathcal{D}_K$, where each $\mathcal{D}_k$ ($k \geq 1$) is produced by finetuning $f_\theta$ on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ and sampling from the resulting model.
9	Depth $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text; depth $d{=}k$ ($k \geq 1$) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-$(k{-}1)$ data.
10	
11	Given a text passage $x$, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth $d \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$.
12	This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and $d{=}1$ is structurally closer to $d{=}0$ than $d{=}3$ is, since each generation step compounds distributional drift.
13	
14	\subsection{Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction}
15	\label{sec:method:benchmark}
16	
17	We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.
18	
19	\paragraph{Model families.}
20	We select three 1--1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2~XL (OpenAI, 1.5B).
21	Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.
22	
23	\paragraph{Decoding strategies.}
24	Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$) \cite{holtzman2020_nucleus}, temperature sampling ($\tau{=}0.9$), and top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$).
25	These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles.
26	Our findings on feature importance and discriminability are limited to this grid; transfer to untested models, scales, or strategies is not established.
27	
28	\paragraph{Depth and scale.}
29	The primary benchmark covers depths d0--d3 across all $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells, with 5{,}000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total).
30	For depth extension experiments (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0--d5.
31	
32	\paragraph{Generation pipeline.}
33	Starting from a Wikipedia subset ($\mathcal{D}_0$), each cycle: (1)~LoRA finetuning \cite{hu2022lora} on $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$ ($r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, lr $2{\times}10^{-4}$, effective batch 16, 3 epochs, dropout $0.05$; fresh adapter from the base model at each depth; full protocol in Appendix~\ref{app:lora_protocol}); (2)~sampling 5{,}000 passages (max 512 tokens, BOS-seeded) under the specified strategy; (3)~$\mathcal{D}_k$ feeds the next cycle.
34	Each depth is produced by a model trained on prior-depth data, not by sampling from the unmodified base model.
35	BOS-seeded generation may amplify depth signal; prompted-generation validation (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) confirms signal persistence ($-$13.8\,pp).
36	No per-passage lineage exists across depths; cross-validation splits do not introduce leakage.
37	
38	\paragraph{Reference model.}
39	All statistical features (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) use Pythia-1.4B as fixed reference model.
40	For Pythia this constitutes self-model measurement, yet its accuracy (78.7\%) does not exceed GPT-2~XL (85.9\%); no systematic self-model advantage is observed.
41	Alternative references (OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) yield 67--79\% (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}); further discussion in Limitations.
42	
43	\subsection{Statistical Feature Design}
44	\label{sec:method:features}
45	
46	We extract a feature vector $\mathbf{f}(x)$ comprising 19 candidate features from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage $x$; ablation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) shows the top 5 achieve 97.6\% of full-set performance, and variance inflation analysis reveals VIF${>}$10 for 14--16 features; effective independent dimensionality is ${\approx}$4--5.
47	The features fall into four categories (Table~\ref{tab:features}).
48	
49	\begin{table}[t]
50	\centering
51	\small
52	\caption{The 19 statistical features comprising $\mathbf{f}(x)$, grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (Pythia-1.4B).}
53	\label{tab:features}
54	\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
55	\toprule
56	Category & Features & $n$ \\
57	\midrule
58	Perplexity & mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, & 9 \\
59	statistics & p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 & \\
60	\addlinespace
61	Surprisal & mean, var, entropy & 3 \\
62	statistics & & \\
63	\addlinespace
64	Lexical & type--token ratio, hapax ratio, & 4 \\
65	diversity & bigram entropy, trigram entropy & \\
66	\addlinespace
67	Repetition & repeated 2/3/4-gram fractions & 3 \\
68	\bottomrule
69	\end{tabular}
70	\end{table}
71	
72	\emph{Perplexity statistics} (9 features) capture the per-token perplexity distribution via moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis) and quantiles (p10--p90); tail quantiles prove especially informative as recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail (\S\ref{sec:atlas}).
73	\emph{Surprisal statistics} (3 features): mean, variance, and entropy of $-\log p(\text{token})$; surprisal variance captures second-order structure not redundant with perplexity moments.
74	\emph{Lexical diversity} (4 features): type--token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram/trigram entropy.
75	\emph{Repetition} (3 features): repeated $n$-gram fractions for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$.
76	
77	\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
78	\label{sec:method:edd}
79	
80	Aggregate multi-class accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depth boundaries.
81	We propose the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) as an operational measure of how far into a recursive chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.
82	
83	\paragraph{Pairwise discriminability.}
84	Let $\mathcal{D} = \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$ denote the depth set and $T \in (0.5, 1.0]$ a discrimination threshold.
85	For each adjacent pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we define the pairwise discriminability $\mathrm{AUC}(d, d{+}1)$ as the area under the ROC curve of a dedicated binary Random Forest classifier (500 trees, $\lfloor\sqrt{19}\rfloor$ candidate features per split) trained on class-balanced data from $\mathbf{f}(x)$ (\S\ref{sec:method:features}) to distinguish depth-$d$ from depth-$(d{+}1)$ samples, evaluated via 5-fold stratified cross-validation.
86	Each pair uses an independent classifier to avoid decision boundary dilution from multi-class settings.
87	
88	\begin{definition}[Effective Discriminable Depth]
89	\label{def:edd}
90	The \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} at threshold $T$ is:
91	\begin{multline}
92	\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 \,:\, \\
93	\forall\, d' \leq d^*,\; \mathrm{AUC}(d', d'{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
94	\label{eq:edd}
95	\end{multline}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics (the 90th-percentile perplexity, \texttt{p90\_ppl}, and surprisal variance, \texttt{var\_surprisal}) emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.
Instruction-tuned variants exhibit monotonically decreasing AUC (regularization), whereas base models can show non-monotonic trajectories; instruction tuning thus acts as a regularizer on the depth signal rather than a source of degradation.

This paper is an empirical study and problem formalization rather than an algorithmic contribution.
We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce a lightweight pipeline: compute 19 reference-model statistical features (effective dimensionality ${\approx}$4--5 due to multicollinearity; \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) and classify with a Random Forest into $K{+}1$ depth classes.
To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K samples).
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and benchmark.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the EDD metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark ($3$ model families $\times$ $3$ decoding strategies $\times$ $4$ depths).

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} Perplexity tail statistics dominate depth discrimination (top-2 in 9/9 and 8/9 cells); $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}4$ for all three families, validated by 5-class (d0--d4) extension on three families (71--80\%); at the stricter $T{=}0.75$, Pythia achieves $p{=}0.001$ with graded confidence across families in the d3--d4 region.

    \item \textbf{Generalization and cross-strategy analysis.} Cross-model LOO 66.4\% (d1--d3: 55.4\%), cross-seed replication across three families, prompted 69.5\%, cross-scale 7--14B (54--70\%, attenuating with scale), cross-domain arXiv 74.1\%. Cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%) reveals a structural difficulty: different decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories, with d1/d2 boundary inversion under strategy mismatch. Surface-text controls (zero-shot LLMs 30--36\%) and binary detection/membership inference baselines (DetectGPT, Min-K\% Prob: 30--33\%) confirm the signal resides in distributional statistics inaccessible from surface text or detection scores.
\end{itemize}
